title: "How"

## Randomisation must be designed in from the start

An RCT is not something that can be added to a programme after launch. The comparison
group, the eligibility rules, and the baseline data all have to be settled before the
first grant is awarded.

[SMART Romania: building the eligibility pool]{.tag}

```{=html}
<div class="flow">
  <div>Outreach<br><span style="font-weight:400;color:#6B6455">Social media, radio, and events in 20+ cities</span></div>
  <div>Online applications<br><span style="font-weight:400;color:#6B6455">About one hour to complete</span></div>
  <div>Automatic screening<br><span style="font-weight:400;color:#6B6455">Stops as soon as a criterion fails</span></div>
  <div style="background:#F2C94C;border-color:#F2C94C">1&nbsp;038 eligible MSMEs<br><span style="font-weight:400">Screened from over 1,500 applicants by September 2023</span></div>
</div>
```

In SMART Romania, one survey did three jobs: application, eligibility check, and
baseline data collection, all in a single step. In October 2023, 519 of the eligible
firms were then randomly selected for funding, and 519 were not.
::::

## Choosing the group size

To detect the impact of a programme, you need enough firms in both the treatment and
comparison groups to reliably tell a real effect apart from the ordinary differences
between firms. Statisticians call this statistical power: with too few firms, even a
programme that works can appear not to. The smaller the effect you want to detect, the
more firms you need. Rules of thumb and power calculations are covered in
[Advanced How](03-advanced-how.qmd).

### Two ways to increase your sample

::: {.cards}
::: {.card-e}
#### Loosen the eligibility bar

If fewer firms qualify than you'd like, lowering the eligibility threshold lets more
firms into the pool you randomise from.
:::
::: {.card-e}
#### Widen the ranking bins

If you're ranking firms by a score, don't treat the ranking as exact. Group
similarly-scored firms into bands, and treat everyone in a band as equally eligible, so
more firms end up in the randomised pool rather than being decided by their exact rank.
:::
:::

::: {.takeaway}
A bigger pool also gives you room to test more than one version of the programme at
once – more on that under Multiple treatment arms, below.
:::

## Five practical ways to randomise your programme

Not every programme fits the same shape. Here are five common ways to randomise one.

```{=html}
<div class="designs">
  <div class="d"><div>
    <h4>Lottery</h4>
    <p><span class="lab">How:</span> randomly select who gets the programme, by public or private lottery.</p>
    <p><span class="lab">Best when:</span> eligibility is clear and the programme is oversubscribed.</p>
  </div></div>
  <div class="d"><div>
    <h4>Multiple treatment arms</h4>
    <p><span class="lab">How:</span> randomly assign different versions of the programme, with or without a control group.</p>
    <p><span class="lab">Best when:</span> you want to know which design works best, not just whether it works.</p>
  </div></div>
  <div class="d"><div>
    <h4>Randomised phase-in</h4>
    <p><span class="lab">How:</span> everyone gets the programme eventually, in a random order. Those still waiting are the comparison group.</p>
    <p><span class="lab">Best when:</span> budget or capacity cannot cover everyone at once.</p>
  </div></div>
  <div class="d"><div>
    <h4>Randomised intensities</h4>
    <p><span class="lab">How:</span> vary how much of the programme a firm gets, for example 100%, 50%, or 0% of eligible employees.</p>
    <p><span class="lab">Best when:</span> spillovers within or between firms are a concern.</p>
  </div></div>
  <div class="d"><div>
    <h4>Encouragement design</h4>
    <p><span class="lab">How:</span> randomise who gets extra outreach to take up the programme, since it cannot be denied to anyone.</p>
    <p><span class="lab">Best when:</span> take-up is voluntary and the programme itself cannot be withheld.</p>
  </div></div>
</div>
```

:::: {.example .romania}
[SMART Romania used a lottery]{.tag}

## Running a lottery: transparency vs. behavioural responses

::: {.compare}
::: {.col-e}
::: {.col-head}
Public lottery
:::
::: {.body}
A public draw, for example pulling names from a hat.

Advantage: transparent and fair.

Disadvantage: the comparison group may change its behaviour once it knows the result.
:::
:::
::: {.col-e}
::: {.col-head}
Private lottery
:::
::: {.body}
A lottery run behind the scenes.

Advantage: avoids the comparison group reacting to a public result.

Disadvantage: less visibly fair.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.takeaway}
In practice, many World Bank-supported evaluations run the draw as a secure, documented,
computerised procedure that can be re-checked afterwards.
:::

Either kind of lottery can also be narrowed to just part of the pool: rather than
randomising everyone who's eligible, you can randomise only the firms near the
eligibility cutoff, and decide the clear-cut cases directly.

## Narrowing the pool: a lottery around a cutoff

Score firms on eligibility criteria. Accept the top scorers outright, reject the bottom
outright, and randomise only the firms in between.

Best when: eligibility criteria are clear and the programme is oversubscribed, with
limited resources.

```{=html}
<figure class="fig-e">
<svg viewBox="0 0 660 300" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" role="img" aria-label="Firms scored from 100 down to 45; the top band is accepted outright, the bottom rejected, and the middle band randomised">
  <text x="20" y="24" fill="#6B6455" font-size="11.5" font-weight="bold">Score</text>

  <rect x="90" y="34" width="280" height="56" rx="5" fill="#F2C94C"/>
  <text x="230" y="60" text-anchor="middle" fill="#2B2724" font-size="13" font-weight="bold">Accept all</text>
  <text x="230" y="78" text-anchor="middle" fill="#2B2724" font-size="11">top scorers funded outright</text>
  <text x="72" y="42" text-anchor="end" fill="#2B2724" font-size="12" font-weight="bold">100</text>
  <text x="72" y="96" text-anchor="end" fill="#2B2724" font-size="12" font-weight="bold">60</text>

  <rect x="90" y="100" width="280" height="76" rx="5" fill="#FFFDF7" stroke="#F2C94C" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="6 4"/>
  <text x="230" y="126" text-anchor="middle" fill="#2B2724" font-size="13" font-weight="bold">Randomise this band</text>
  <text x="230" y="145" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6B6455" font-size="11">85% treatment, 15% comparison</text>
  <text x="230" y="163" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6B6455" font-size="11">this band is the sample for study</text>
  <text x="72" y="182" text-anchor="end" fill="#2B2724" font-size="12" font-weight="bold">45</text>

  <rect x="90" y="186" width="280" height="52" rx="5" fill="#FFFDF7" stroke="#E4DCC6"/>
  <text x="230" y="210" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6B6455" font-size="13" font-weight="bold">Reject all</text>
  <text x="230" y="228" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6B6455" font-size="11">below the eligibility bar</text>

  <path d="M382 138 H410" stroke="#B9AF95" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <rect x="410" y="106" width="230" height="64" rx="5" fill="rgba(242,201,76,.16)"/>
  <text x="425" y="128" fill="#2B2724" font-size="11.5" font-weight="bold">Only the middle band is randomised</text>
  <text x="425" y="146" fill="#6B6455" font-size="11">The strongest and weakest applicants</text>
  <text x="425" y="160" fill="#6B6455" font-size="11">are handled by the score, not the draw</text>

  <text x="20" y="270" fill="#6B6455" font-size="11.5">Example: credit scoring in the Philippines</text>
</svg>
</figure>
```

::: {.caution}
Keep selection rules-based. Subjective rankings, even by judges or expert panels, have
been shown to introduce hidden bias that a lottery or scored cutoff avoids.
:::

## Rule-based scoring beats judgment-based scoring

Across several studies, subjective judgment struggles to identify future winners.

::: {.cards}
::: {.card-e}
#### Judges favour their own group

A study of court rulings in Kenya found that defendants were more likely to win if they
shared the judge's ethnicity or gender.

Chen, Daniel L., et al., "Do Judges Favour Their Own Ethnicity and Gender?" (2022).
:::
::: {.card-e}
#### Judges do not beat a simple survey

In a business plan competition, a short applicant survey predicted future firm growth
slightly better than expert judge panels did on their own.

Fafchamps, Marcel, and Christopher Woodruff, "Identifying gazelles: Expert panels vs.
surveys," *World Bank Economic Review* 31(3) (2017).
:::
::: {.card-e}
#### Judges, and algorithms, both struggle

Comparing judges' scores, researcher prediction models, and machine learning in a
Nigerian business competition, none of the three approaches predicted which firms
actually survived, grew, or turned a profit three years later.

McKenzie, David, and Dario Sansone, "Predicting entrepreneurial success is hard,"
*Journal of Development Economics* 141 (2019).
:::
:::

::: {.takeaway}
Subjective judgment, even from experts, struggles to reliably pick future winners. This
is part of why rules-based methods – lotteries or scored cutoffs – are often the fairer
and more defensible way to allocate a programme, rather than discretionary picks.
:::

## Multiple treatment arms: testing programme versions

Randomly assign firms (or CEOs, employees) to different versions of the programme, and
compare them against each other and against the comparison group. This also works
without a comparison group at all, if you only want to compare versions.

Best when: you're uncertain which component or design actually drives results, and
want to know which version works best, not just whether the programme works.

Advantage: helps investigate the channels of impact.
Trade-off: needs a larger sample size, since it's split across more groups.

```{=html}
<figure class="fig-e">
<svg viewBox="0 0 660 240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" role="img" aria-label="Bar chart comparing outcomes across a comparison group and three programme versions">

  <text x="570" y="25" text-anchor="middle" fill="#2B2724" font-size="13" font-weight="bold">4.5</text>
```

## Randomised phase-in: everyone gets it, just not at once

Everybody eventually receives the programme, just at different, randomly assigned
times. Whoever is scheduled last serves as the comparison group in the meantime. Leave
enough time between waves for impacts to develop.

Best when: budget, time, or capacity constraints mean you can't roll the programme
out to everyone at once.

Advantages: everyone eventually receives the programme, which makes the decision
transparent and easier to justify; it also lets you study how impact changes with
different treatment durations.
Trade-off: you can't observe long-term impacts, since the comparison group
eventually receives the programme too.

```{=html}
<figure class="fig-e">
<svg viewBox="0 0 660 200" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" role="img" aria-label="Staggered rollout: wave one treated first, wave two later, wave three last, each acting as comparison until treated">

  <rect x="110" y="30" width="510" height="26" fill="#F2C94C"/>

  <text x="20" y="90" fill="#2B2724" font-size="12" font-weight="bold">Wave 2</text>

  <rect x="280" y="74" width="340" height="26" fill="#F2C94C"/>

  <text x="20" y="134" fill="#2B2724" font-size="12" font-weight="bold">Wave 3</text>
  <rect x="110" y="118" width="340" height="26" fill="#DDD5C0"/>
  <rect x="450" y="118" width="170" height="26" fill="#F2C94C"/>

  <line x1="110" y1="160" x2="620" y2="160" stroke="#B9AF95" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <text x="620" y="178" text-anchor="end" fill="#6B6455" font-size="11.5">Time</text>

  <rect x="110" y="182" width="11" height="11" fill="#F2C94C"/>
  <text x="128" y="192" fill="#6B6455" font-size="11.5">Treated</text>
  <rect x="210" y="182" width="11" height="11" fill="#DDD5C0"/>
  <text x="228" y="192" fill="#6B6455" font-size="11.5">Waiting, acts as comparison</text>
</svg>
</figure>
```

## Randomised intensities: varying how much firms get

Randomly vary how much of the programme each firm gets: for example, some firms get it
for 100% of eligible employees, others for only part, e.g. 50%, and others none at all
(the comparison group).

Best when: spillovers are likely – for example, information spreading between
treated and untreated employees within the same firm.

Advantage: lets you analyse possible spillovers, not just the direct effect.
Trade-off: needs a bigger sample size to detect effects at each intensity level.

```{=html}
<figure class="fig-e">
<svg viewBox="0 0 660 210" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" role="img" aria-label="Three firms receive the programme at 100 percent, 50 percent and zero percent of eligible employees">
  <line x1="120" y1="165" x2="600" y2="165" stroke="#B9AF95" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <rect x="150" y="35" width="110" height="130" fill="#F2C94C"/>
  <text x="205" y="106" text-anchor="middle" fill="#2B2724" font-size="15" font-weight="bold">100%</text>
  <text x="205" y="185" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6B6455" font-size="12">Firm A</text>

  <rect x="300" y="100" width="110" height="65" fill="#F2C94C"/>
  <text x="355" y="138" text-anchor="middle" fill="#2B2724" font-size="15" font-weight="bold">50%</text>
  <text x="355" y="185" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6B6455" font-size="12">Firm B</text>

  <rect x="450" y="140" width="110" height="25" fill="#DDD5C0"/>
  <text x="505" y="132" text-anchor="middle" fill="#2B2724" font-size="15" font-weight="bold">0%</text>
  <text x="505" y="185" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6B6455" font-size="12">Firm C</text>

  <text x="120" y="22" fill="#6B6455" font-size="11.5">Share of eligible employees within each firm who receive the programme</text>
</svg>
</figure>
```

## Facing low take-up? Randomise the encouragement

The problem: low take-up. The firms who need a programme most can be the least
likely to take it up – badly managed firms often don't know they're badly managed. Low
take-up also makes it hard to tell whether a programme is working.

Solution: encouragement design. When you can't deny the programme to anyone – for
example, an open voucher scheme – randomise who gets extra outreach or information
encouraging them to take it up, then compare the encouraged group with the
not-encouraged group.

Advantage: works even when everyone must have access to the programme.
Trade-off: only captures part of the impact, and can be biased if untargeted
encouragement – TV or radio, for example – reaches the comparison group too.

::: {.caution}
Compliance is rarely perfect: some encouraged firms never take up the programme, and
some not-encouraged firms take it up anyway. Compare the whole encouraged group with the
whole not-encouraged group regardless.
:::

## Still not convinced? More arguments for randomising

::: {.cards}
::: {.card-e}
#### Free and fair competition

The researcher determines allocation, not personal connections or favouritism, so
there's no selection bias – no systematic difference between groups on average. It can
be designed to answer precisely the question you need answered, especially when the
effect of a policy is uncertain.
:::
::: {.card-e}
#### Equality and non-discrimination

Often the outcome of a policy isn't clear, and it could even be negative. Testing first,
rather than rolling it out to everyone, protects people from that uncertainty. You can
also make sure everyone still receives the core programme, and only randomise an add-on
whose effect isn't yet known.
:::
::: {.card-e}
#### Publicity and transparency

A randomised design needs fewer additional assumptions than other evaluation methods.
Because the analysis is less complex, it's easier to explain and defend the findings to
the people affected by them.
